title: Audio Fundamentals — Waveforms, Sampling, Fourier Transform

questions.question: How many samples does sine(440.0, sr=8000, seconds=0.064) create?
questions.explanation: The function uses n=int(sr*seconds), so 8000*0.064 gives 512 samples.

questions.question: What is the frequency-bin spacing for the 512-sample, 8 kHz DFT in the demo?
options: 8 Hz
512 Hz
125 Hz
questions.explanation: DFT resolution is sr/N = 8000/512 = 15.625 Hz per bin.

questions.question: What does mix(s1, s2) do when the signals have different lengths?
options: It keeps only the longer signal
It pads the shorter signal with zeros and sums without scaling
It stops at the shorter length and averages the samples at each index
It interleaves alternating samples from both signals
questions.explanation: mix uses min(len(s)) and returns the arithmetic mean of the signals at each retained position.

questions.question: A 7 kHz tone sampled at 10 kHz is above Nyquist. Which peak does peak_freq report?
options: 10 kHz
7 kHz
5 kHz
3 kHz
questions.explanation: The sampled tone aliases to sr-f = 10000-7000 = 3000 Hz, below the 5 kHz Nyquist limit.

questions.question: Why does downsample_naive(sig, factor=3) make a 7 kHz tone at 24 kHz appear near 1 kHz?
options: Decimation without low-pass filtering folds energy above the new 4 kHz Nyquist frequency
The DFT always divides frequencies by three after sampling
The sine generator changes its frequency when a slice is taken
WAV quantization removes every frequency above 1 kHz
questions.explanation: After decimation the sample rate is 8 kHz; the original 7 kHz component aliases to 8-7 = 1 kHz.

questions.question: What error is introduced by write_wav followed by read_wav in the demo?
options: A guaranteed one-second time shift
Small 16-bit quantization error from converting float samples to signed integers
A change from mono to stereo
A new DFT phase chosen at random
questions.explanation: write_wav stores scaled 16-bit integers, so read_wav cannot recover every original floating-point sample exactly.
